title: Association between nighttime sleep duration and falls among community-dwelling older adults aged 65 and over: findings from a nationwide population-based study

sections.abstract:
It’s well established that falls are a leading cause of injury among older adults and may be influenced by sleep duration. This study aimed to investigate the association between nighttime sleep duration and fall risk in a nationally representative older population.

This population-based cross-sectional study used data from the Turkey Older adults Profile Survey conducted in 2023. A total of 10,321 community-dwelling adults aged 65 years and older were included. Data on demographics, health characteristics, sleep duration, environmental factors, and fall history were collected through structured interviews. Univariable and multivariable logistic regression models were undertaken to estimate the association between nighttime sleep duration (< 7 h, 7–8 h [reference], and > 8 h) and falls. Multivariable models progressively adjusted for age, gender, education, marital status, physical activity, BMI, alcohol use, regular medication, walking difficulty, visual impairment, depression, chronic disease status, self-rated health, and environmental factors. Odds ratios (OR) and adjusted odds ratios (aOR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated.

Among the participants (mean age: 72.8 ± 6.4 years; 54.5% female), 20.1% reported falls in the past year. Short sleep duration (< 7 h) was associated with significantly increased odds of falling in both unadjusted (OR = 1.755, 95% CI: 1.584–1.944, p < 0.001) and fully adjusted models (aOR = 1.546, 95% CI: 1.388–1.724, p < 0.001). Long sleep duration (> 8 h) initially indicated an elevated fall risk (OR = 1.224, 95% CI: 1.036–1.447, p = 0.018); however, this association lost statistical significance after fully adjusting for several health and environmental covariates (aOR = 1.091, 95% CI: 0.918–1.297, p = 0.322).

Nighttime sleep duration less than 7 h was independently associated with an increased risk of falls among older adults. Interventions promoting optimal sleep duration could be a crucial component of fall prevention strategies targeting older populations.
sections.introduction:
It’s a well-known fact that the transition from infectious to non-communicable diseases, along with advancements in modern healthcare services, has led to an increase in the proportion of the older adults population [ 1 ]. By 2030, it is projected that one in every six people worldwide will be aged 60 years or older [ 2 – 4 ]. Similarly, Türkiye is also becoming an increasingly aging society [ 5 ]. As of 2024, the proportion of the population aged 65 and over in Türkiye is 10.6% of the total population [ 6 , 7 ]. This proportion is projected to increase to 23.1% by 2050 and 31.7% by 2075 [ 5 – 7 ].

Falls in older adults individuals, although often preventable, can lead to significant health losses and even fatalities [ 8 ]. Injuries resulting from falls negatively affect the individual’s ability to maintain independent living, leading to limitations in daily activities and a decrease in quality of life [ 9 ]. Research shows that one in every three older adults individuals aged 65 and over, and half of those aged 85 and over, fall at least once a year [ 10 ]. A large proportion of these falls result in physical injuries, with approximately 10% leading to severe trauma [ 11 ]. After a fall, individuals may experience a decrease in self-care capacity, a decline in social interactions, and loss of independence, which can negatively affect mental health [ 12 ].

The occurrence of falls is usually not due to a single cause, but rather results from the simultaneous interaction of various factors [ 13 ]. These risk factors can be categorized into three groups: the individual’s health status and functional capacity (intrinsic), environmental conditions (extrinsic), and circumstances related to activities performed (situational) [ 13 ]. Among the risk factors frequently mentioned in the literature are weakness in the lower extremity muscles, a history of previous falls, balance and gait disorders, use of assistive devices, vision problems, the presence of arthritis, loss of independence in daily living activities, depression, cognitive impairment, advanced age, and the use of certain medications, and urge-type urinary incontinence [ 14 – 16 ]. Studies conducted in China and South Africa reported fall prevalence rates of 19.3% and 32.6%, respectively [ 17 , 18 ]. In these studies, falls have been found to be associated with factors such as age, gender, marital status, presence of chronic diseases, physical disability, education level, medication use, and cognitive status [ 17 , 18 ]. Additionally, lower education levels, the use of antidepressant or antidiabetic medications, and being divorced or widowed have been found to increase the risk of falls [ 17 , 18 ].

In addition to these risk factors, recent years have seen a growing interest in exploring the relationship between sleep disorders and falls among older adults [ 19 , 20 ]. Changes in sleep patterns are known to be a natural consequence of aging, and sleep problems become more common in later life. During this period, the duration and depth of nighttime sleep tend to decrease, while daytime napping, the number of nighttime awakenings, and the total time spent awake during the night increase [ 21 ].

Sleep disturbances are highly prevalent among community-dwelling older adults, with global estimates ranging from 30% to 70% [ 22 ]. Despite the rapid increase in the older adults population in Turkey, studies examining the relationship between sleep duration and fall risk among older adults are limited, and the few existing studies have generally been conducted on small samples that do not adequately represent community-dwelling older adults [ 23 , 24 ]. Additionally, studies examining the relationship between sleep duration or sleep disturbances and falls among older adults have yielded inconsistent findings [ 19 , 20 ]. Some studies have reported a significant ‘U-shaped’ relationship, indicating that both short and long sleep durations increase the risk of falls [ 25 , 26 ], whereas others have found associations only with short or long sleep duration [ 27 – 29 ]. The sociocultural, environmental, and health profiles of older adults in Turkey may differ from those in other countries [ 30 ], which could influence the association between sleep duration and falls. Furthermore, research in this field, particularly among community-dwelling older populations, remains limited both globally and in Turkey. In this context, the aim of this study is to examine the association between self-reported nighttime sleep duration and falls among older adults in Turkey.
sections.methods:
This population-based cross-sectional study is based on secondary data analysis. The database of the Turkey Older adults Profile Survey, conducted for the first time in 2023, was used in this research [ 31 ]. The Turkey Older adults Profile Survey, which reflects the older adult population in Turkey, was carried out by the Turkish Statistical Institute and the Ministry of Family and Social Services to develop policies related to the older adults [ 31 ]. The sampling method of this study was determined as multistage cluster sampling. The sample selection process of the study consists of two stages. In the first stage, cluster blocks consisting of an average of 100 household addresses, each containing at least one individual aged 50 and above, were defined according to the Address-Based Population Registration System (ADNKS), and were randomly selected with probability proportional to size. In this context, 2,264 clusters were randomly selected, completing the first stage [ 31 ]. In the second stage, systematic random sampling was used to select household addresses from the clusters identified in the first stage [ 31 ]. Ten households were randomly selected from each cluster and included in the study. The sample size of the research covers Turkey as a whole and the 12 regions identified according to the Statistical Regional Units Classification (SRUC) Level 1. Within the scope of the study, 22,640 households, each containing at least one individual aged 50 or above, were determined as the sample households. Data was collected from 29,785 individuals aged 50 and above living in the selected households (14,044 men and 15,741 women). In this study, data from 10,321 individuals aged 65 and over were analyzed [ 31 ]. The multistage cluster sampling method and participant selection process used in this study are detailed in Fig. 1 .

Fig. 1 A flow diagram illustrating the selection procedure of community-dwelling older adults aged 65 and over

A flow diagram illustrating the selection procedure of community-dwelling older adults aged 65 and over

In this study, the presence of falls was considered the dependent variable. Participants were asked, “Have you fallen in the past 12 months?” and responses were categorized as “Yes” or “No.” Nighttime sleep duration was assessed by asking participants, “How many hours do you sleep at night?”. Responses were categorized as < 7 h (short sleep), 7–8 h (normal sleep), and > 8 h (long sleep), in accordance with established clinical recommendations and prior epidemiological studies [ 23 , 27 , 32 ] identifying 7–8 h as the optimal sleep duration for adults and shorter or longer durations as potentially adverse [ 33 ]. Furthermore, the independent variables were grouped into four categories: sociodemographic, intrinsic, extrinsic, and situational factors [ 13 , 34 ].

Sociodemographic factors: Participants were divided into two age groups: 65–74 years and 75 years or older. Sex was categorized as male and female. Educational status was categorized into three groups: low, medium, and high education level. Participants who were illiterate, had not completed any school, or had completed only primary school, general middle school, elementary education, or vocational and technical middle school were considered to have a low education level. Those who graduated from high school or vocational high school were classified as having a medium education level. Participants with associate, bachelor’s, or postgraduate degrees were considered to have a high education level. Marital status was assessed through the question “What is your marital status?” with response options categorized as “Never married,” “Married,” “Divorced,” “Widowed,” and “Unknown.” For analysis, this variable was grouped into “Married” and “Not married” (including never married, divorced, and widowed). Living alone was assessed by the question, “Do you live alone in this household?” with “Yes” and “No” response options.

Intrinsic factors: Vision status was evaluated based on responses to the question, “Do you have difficulty seeing (even if you use glasses or contact lenses)?” The response options were “No difficulty,” “Some difficulty,” “A lot of difficulty,” and “Cannot do at all.” For analysis, these were grouped into two categories: “No, does not have difficulty” (including “No difficulty” and “Some difficulty”) and “Yes, has difficulty” (including “A lot of difficulty” and “Cannot do at all”). Depression in the Turkey Aging Profile Survey was measured using the Geriatric Depression Scale. Depression in the Turkey Aging Profile Survey was measured using the GDS. Originally developed by Yesavage et al. (1982) [ 35 ] to assess depressive symptoms in older adults, the GDS includes 30 items with “yes/no” response options. Its original Cronbach’s alpha reliability coefficient was 0.94. The Turkish adaptation and validation, conducted by Ertan et al. (1997) [ 36 ], yielded a Cronbach’s alpha of 0.92. Each depression-oriented answer receives 1 point, while the other response option is scored as 0, resulting in a total depression score ranging from 0 to 30. Based on total scores, respondents are categorized as “not depressed” (0–9 points), “mildly depressed” (10–19 points), or “severely depressed” (≥ 20 points). Additionally, a dichotomous variable was created for regression analyses, whereby participants with a GDS-30 score of ≥ 10 were classified as having depressive symptoms, a commonly accepted threshold indicating clinically relevant depression in older adults. Presence of chronic disease was evaluated with the question, “Do you have any chronic (long-term) diseases such as hypertension, diabetes, heart disease, cancer, kidney failure, stroke, hepatitis, asthma, etc.?” with “Yes” and “No” responses. Subjective health status was assessed by the question, “How would you describe your general health?” using a five-point Likert scale (Very good, Good, Fair, Poor, Very poor). For analysis, responses were grouped into “Good” (Very good and Good) and “Poor” (Fair, Poor, and Very poor). Medication use was assessed by the question, “Do you regularly take any prescribed medication(s)?” with “Yes” and “No” responses. Walking difficulty was evaluated through the question, “Do you have difficulty walking, or going up or down stairs?” with response options of “No difficulty,” “Some difficulty,” “A lot of difficulty,” and “Cannot do at all.” For analysis, responses were grouped into “No, does not have difficulty” (including “No difficulty” and “Some difficulty”) and “Yes, has difficulty” (including “A lot of difficulty” and “Cannot do at all”).

Extrinsic factors: Medication use was assessed by the question, “Do you regularly take any prescribed medication(s)?” with “Yes” and “No” responses. Difficulty due to lack of grab bars in the bathroom or toilet was assessed by the question, “Do you have difficulty due to the lack of grab bars in your toilet or bathroom at home?” with “Yes” and “No” response options. Difficulty due to the height of the kitchen counter was assessed with the question, “Do you experience difficulty due to the height of your kitchen counter at home?” Similarly, difficulty due to high door thresholds was assessed with the question, “Do you experience difficulty due to the high thresholds of the doors at home?” and difficulty with steps or stairs was assessed with the question, “Do you experience difficulty due to the height of the steps or stairs at home?” Each of these variables was analyzed based on “Yes” and “No” responses.

Situational factors: Physical activity level was determined by the participants’ responses to the question, “How often do you engage in physical activity, exercise, or sports?” Responses of “Every day or almost every day” and “At least once a week (but not every day)” were categorized as physically active; responses of “1–3 times per month,” “Rarely,” and “Never” were classified as inactive. Alcohol consumption was assessed with the question, “Do you consume alcoholic beverages?” with “Yes” and “No” response options.

Statistical analyses were conducted using IBM SPSS Statistics version 30.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA) and Stata version 18.0 (StataCorp LLC, College Station, TX, USA). Descriptive statistics were presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD) for continuous variables and frequencies with percentages (%) for categorical variables. Normality of continuous data distributions was assessed by visual inspection of histograms and the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test. Univariable logistic regression analyses were initially performed to examine associations between nighttime sleep duration categories (< 7 h, 7–8 h [reference], and > 8 h) and the likelihood of reporting falls within the past year, with results reported as crude odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Subsequently, multivariable logistic regression models were conducted to adjust for potential confounders. Four sequentially adjusted models were constructed: Model 1: Unadjusted model; Model 2: Adjusted for demographic factors, including age, gender, education level, and marital status; Model 3: Further adjusted for health-related variables, such as physical activity, body mass index (BMI), alcohol use, regular medication use, walking difficulties, visual impairment, depressive symptoms, chronic disease status, and self-rated health; Model 4: Additionally adjusted for environmental risk factors, including the presence of high kitchen counters, high door thresholds, difficulty with stairs or steps, and lack of grab bars in bathrooms or toilets. In addition, stratified univariable and multivariable logistic regression analyses were conducted to examine whether the association between nighttime sleep duration and falls differed by depression status. Adjusted odds ratios (aORs) and corresponding 95% CIs were calculated for each sleep duration category. Model diagnostics were conducted to check for multicollinearity among covariates by evaluating variance inflation factors (VIF), where VIF values < 5 were deemed acceptable. Hosmer–Lemeshow goodness-of-fit tests were performed to evaluate model calibration, and the models demonstrated adequate fit ( p > 0.05). All analyses were two-tailed, and missing data were minimal (< 2% per variable); thus, complete-case analyses were employed without imputation. Statistical significance for all analyses was defined utilizing a two-tailed value threshold set at p < 0.05.
sections.results:
Figure 1 presents a step‑wise flow diagram summarizing the sampling and data‑cleaning process for the study cohort. In the identification phase, a two‑stage cluster design initially targeted 2,264 clusters comprising 22,640 household addresses, yielding a pool of 29,787 potential respondents. During screening, all individuals younger than 65 years ( n = 18,130) were excluded to restrict the analysis to the older‑adult population, leaving 11,657 completed data forms. A subsequent quality check identified missing information on key study variables in 1,336 cases (11.5% of the age‑eligible sample); these records were removed to ensure analytic integrity through complete‑case analysis. The resulting sample consisted of 10,321 community‑dwelling adults aged ≥ 65 years, representing 87.5% of the initially eligible respondents and 34.6% of the original target population.

The mean age of the participants was 72.8 ± 6.4 years, and 54.5% were female [Table 1 ]. Among the participants, 65.3% were married, and 83.6% had a low level of education. A total of 78.5% of the individuals had at least one chronic disease, and 20.6% were living alone. Regarding physical activity, 71.2% were inactive. Regular or prescribed medication use was reported by 78.8% of the participants [Table 1 ]. A history of falls in the past year was reported by 20.1% of the participants, and 20.1% also reported walking difficulties. The most common nighttime sleep duration was 7–8 h (55.2%), followed by < 7 h (34.5%) and > 8 h (10.3%) [Table 2 ]. Mild symptoms of depression were present in 34.2% of participants, while 12.5% had severe depressive symptoms. Details of sociodemographic and health-related characteristics are presented in Tables 1 and 2 .

Compared to the reference group (older adults sleeping 7–8 h at night), those sleeping less than 7 h had a 75.5% higher risk of falls in the unadjusted model (OR = 1.755, 95% CI: 1.584–1.944, p < 0.001). Similarly, individuals sleeping more than 8 h showed a 22.4% increased risk (OR = 1.224, 95% CI = 1.036–1.447) [Table 3 ]. After adjustment for age, gender, education, and marital status (Model 2), the risk remained similarly elevated, with a 75.6% higher fall risk for those sleeping less than 7 h (aOR = 1.758, 95% CI = 1.586–1.947, p < 0.001) and a 22.5% increased risk for those sleeping more than 8 h (aOR = 1.227, 95% CI = 1.038–1.451, p = 0.016) [Table 3 ]. In Model 3, which further adjusted for physical activity, BMI, alcohol use, regular medication, walking difficulty, visual impairment, depression, chronic disease status, and self-rated health, the risk of falls was 54.5% higher among those sleeping less than 7 h (aOR = 1.546, 95% CI = 1.390–1.719, p < 0.001), while the increased risk for those sleeping more than 8 h was 9.1% and not statistically significant (aOR = 1.093, 95% CI = 0.919–1.299, p = 0.314). Finally, in Model 4, after additional adjustment for environmental factors such as kitchen counter height, high door thresholds, difficulty with stairs, and lack of grab bars in bathrooms or toilets, the risk remained 54.5% higher for the short sleep group (aOR = 1.546, 95% CI = 1.388–1.724, p < 0.001), and the slight increase in risk among those sleeping more than 8 h remained non-significant (aOR = 1.091, 95% CI = 0.918–1.297, p = 0.322). The Hosmer–Lemeshow goodness‑of‑fit tests indicated adequate calibration for all models (Model 2: χ²=12.293, p = 0.139; Model 3: χ²=12.570, Model 4: p = 0.128; χ² = 7.734, p = 0.454), as p -values exceeded 0.05, suggesting no evidence of lack‑of‑fit. All independent variables had VIFs < 5, indicating no evidence of problematic multicollinearity.

Short nighttime sleep duration (< 7 h) is consistently associated with an elevated risk of falls in both depressed and non-depressed older adults (Table 4 ). In the fully adjusted models, individuals without depression who sleep < 7 h have a 1.64-fold higher odds of falling (aOR = 1.646; 95% CI: 1.422–1.904, p < 0.001), while those with depression show a similarly increased risk (aOR = 1.445; 95% CI: 1.236–1.690, p < 0.001). In contrast, long sleep duration (> 8 h) is not significantly associated with falls in either group, with effect estimates remaining close to null (aORs ≈ 1.07–1.10, p > 0.05). Notably, all fully adjusted models demonstrate adequate goodness-of-fit according to Hosmer–Lemeshow statistics, supporting the reliability of the estimated associations.

sections.discussion:
Falls are a major geriatric health concern and one of the leading causes of injury and mortality in older adults [ 20 ]. Growing evidence indicates that sleep duration may be a modifiable risk factor for falls in this population [ 37 ]. Furthermore, the present findings emphasize that modifiable sleep characteristics can influence fall risk, adding to evidence that poor sleep quality—particularly insufficient sleep duration—is associated with significantly higher odds of falls in older populations [ 38 ]. In this population-based cross-sectional study of 10,321 community-dwelling adults aged ≥ 65, we found that those sleeping less than 7 h per night had approximately a 1.5-fold higher odds of experiencing a fall compared to those sleeping 7–8 h. By contrast, an initially observed slight increase in fall risk among long sleepers (> 8 h) was not statistically significant after adjusting for demographic, health, and environmental covariates. These results suggest that insufficient nighttime sleep is independently associated with elevated fall risk in older adults, reinforcing prior findings that short sleep duration is a significant contributor to falls in this age group [ 25 ]. From a policy perspective on aging and older adults care, these results highlight the need to incorporate sleep health into comprehensive fall-prevention strategies and guidelines, aligning with the global imperative to prioritize fall prevention as populations age.

The strong link between short sleep and falls in our study aligns with a broad literature identifying insufficient sleep as a significant fall risk factor in older adults [ 39 ]. For instance, a large cohort analysis confirmed that sleep problems (e.g. very short sleep or frequent insomnia symptoms) were associated with increased fall rates even after accounting for the use of sedative medications [ 40 ]. Similarly, poor sleep quality and fragmentation have been tied to impaired balance and higher fall propensity; in one study, older adults with frequent sleep disturbances had ~ 30% greater odds of falling [ 38 ]. Mechanistically, chronic sleep deprivation can cause daytime somnolence, slowed reaction times, and cognitive impairment, which collectively increase the likelihood of falls [ 41 ]. In fact, older adults with persistent insomnia demonstrate slower gait speed and worse dual-task cognitive performance than good sleepers, providing a plausible pathway by which sleep loss leads to instability and falls [ 41 ].

In contrast to short sleep, the association between long sleep duration and falls was weaker and lost significance after full adjustment in our models – a pattern also noted in some prior studies [ 42 ]. Admittedly, certain analyses have reported that very long sleepers (for example, ≥ 9–10 h) show higher fall incidence, though the effect sizes tend to be modest compared to short sleep [ 25 ]. One recent study found that long sleep was linked to greater fall risk only among older adults with cardiovascular disease, suggesting that underlying health status can modify this relationship [ 39 ]. It is likely that prolonged sleep is a marker of underlying vulnerabilities—such as frailty, depression, or multiple chronic conditions—which themselves predispose individuals to falls [ 37 ]. Consistent with this interpretation, our findings and other epidemiological evidence indicate that extended sleep per se is not an independent risk factor for falls once comorbidities are taken into account, in clear contrast to the robust impact of short sleep [ 42 ].

The bidirectional interplay between sleep and mood is well documented in older adults: chronic insomnia can exacerbate depressive symptoms, and conversely, major depression often presents with characteristic sleep disturbances. In practice, this means that an older adults person with persistent insomnia is more vulnerable to developing or worsening depression, while a depressed elder frequently shows fragmented sleep, reduced slow-wave sleep, and shortened REM latency. This vicious cycle promotes accelerated functional decline, since both chronic sleep loss and depression are independently linked to cognitive impairment, physical frailty, and disability in seniors [ 16 , 43 – 45 ]. Of note, insomnia and depression share overlapping neurobiological and psychosocial pathways (for example, chronic stress/inflammation and impaired arousal regulation), suggesting that their co-occurrence can have synergistic effects on balance and gait. Clinically, older adults with both sleep disturbance and depression have markedly higher fall rates than those with either condition alone, in part because depressive affect (and related anxiety/fear of falling) further impairs postural control and attention via cognitive and motor pathways. Thus, the reciprocal insomnia–depression nexus in frail elders may substantially increase fall susceptibility by accelerating cognitive–motor decline. Our results suggest that depression may slightly attenuate—but does not eliminate—the effect of short sleep on fall risk, supporting the notion that depressive symptomatology interacts with sleep-related physiological and behavioral mechanisms. Depression may influence the relationship between sleep and falls through several interrelated mechanisms. Cognitive impairment, psychomotor slowing, and diminished attentional control—common in late-life depression—can undermine balance and situational awareness, increasing susceptibility to falls [ 46 , 47 ]. Additionally, depression-related fatigue and daytime sleepiness may further impair physical reactivity and gait stability [ 38 , 48 ]. In our study, although short sleep duration (< 7 h) increased fall risk in both groups, the association was stronger in those without depression (aOR = 1.646) compared to those with depression (aOR = 1.445). This may reflect that in individuals without depressive symptoms, the impact of sleep deprivation manifests more directly, whereas in depressed individuals, multiple overlapping risk factors (e.g., cognitive dysfunction, medication use) may partially mask the independent contribution of sleep duration to fall risk. These findings suggest that depression both interacts with and modulates the sleep–falls pathway, highlighting the need for integrated mental health and sleep assessments in geriatric fall prevention.

Taken together, our findings suggest that maintaining a moderate nightly sleep duration (around 7–8 h) is optimal for minimizing fall risk in older adults [ 39 ]. Short sleep duration, in particular, emerged as an independent and modifiable risk factor for falls; this highlights the potential benefit of interventions to improve sleep duration and quality as part of comprehensive fall prevention strategies [ 38 ]. Incorporating routine sleep assessments into geriatric care may help identify high-risk individuals, as both sleep problems and related factors (like fatigue or pain) are tractable targets for intervention in order to reduce falls. Ultimately, addressing sleep insufficiency in the older adults through behavioral sleep therapies, sleep hygiene education, or management of underlying conditions could complement existing multifactorial fall prevention efforts and improve the health and safety of our aging population.

Of note, urinary incontinence may also represent a plausible pathway linking sleep disturbance to increased fall risk in older adults [ 15 , 49 , 50 ]. Nocturia-related awakenings can fragment sleep and prompt rushed nighttime toileting, particularly in low-light environments, thereby elevating fall susceptibility. Although our study could not assess urinary incontinence directly due to data limitations, this mechanism remains clinically relevant and warrants investigation in future research to more fully elucidate the behavioral and physiological pathways connecting sleep patterns with fall risk.

A strength of this study is that it is the nationally representative investigation in Turkey to examine the association between nighttime sleep duration and falls among community-dwelling older adults. Another strength of this study is its large, population-based sample and the comprehensive adjustment for confounders, including less-studied factors like home environmental hazards (e.g. lack of grab bars or high steps) that can contribute to falls. Second, another strong point of the study is the very low proportion of missing data (< 2% per variable). Third, all independent variables had VIFs < 5, indicating no evidence of problematic multicollinearity. Given the large sample size, the non-significant results further support that predicted probabilities align reasonably well with observed outcomes. However, the cross-sectional design limits causal inference. Furthermore, logistic regression can only identify associations rather than establish causality. It remains possible that poor health leads to both sleep disturbances and falls (reverse causation). Sleep duration was based on self-reported data without objective verification. While practical in large population surveys, self-reported measures are subject to recall or reporting bias and may misestimate actual sleep duration, as well as fail to capture sleep quality or specific disorders such as sleep apnea and insomnia. Hence, other important sleep-related parameters, such as sleep quality, sleep efficiency, daytime sleepiness, and the presence of specific sleep disorders, were not evaluated. As these factors may independently affect balance, cognition, and fall risk in older adults, their omission may have contributed to residual confounding. Future studies incorporating comprehensive and multidimensional sleep assessments are warranted to better elucidate the relationship between sleep and falls. Notably, another important limitation of this study is the lack of detailed data on the use of sedative or hypnotic medications, such as benzodiazepines or Z-drugs. These agents are known to alter sleep architecture, reduce arousal thresholds, and impair balance and cognition, thereby independently increasing the risk of falls in older adults. Given their frequent use in geriatric populations to manage insomnia or anxiety, it is possible that some of the observed associations between short sleep and falls may be partially mediated or confounded by pharmacologic factors. Future studies should incorporate medication-specific data to better isolate the effects of sleep patterns from those of sedative use. Another limitation of this study is that frailty status, which is a well-established prognostic factor for falls in older adults, was not directly assessed in the present study. Frailty reflects a multidimensional vulnerability encompassing physical, cognitive, and functional domains and may modify the association between exposures and fall risk. The absence of a standardized frailty measure may therefore have led to residual confounding and limited our ability to fully capture individual vulnerability to falls. Future studies incorporating validated frailty indices or phenotype-based assessments are warranted to better elucidate the interplay between frailty, depressive symptoms, sleep characteristics, and fall outcomes. Moreover, regular medication use was assessed using a binary indicator (yes/no), which did not allow for the evaluation of polypharmacy based on the number or types of medications. Given that polypharmacy is a well-established risk factor for falls in older adults, the lack of detailed medication data may have resulted in residual confounding. Future studies should incorporate comprehensive medication assessments to better characterize the impact of polypharmacy on fall risk. Despite these limitations, the findings of this study have important implications for public health and healthy aging. In rapidly aging societies such as Turkey, identifying modifiable risk factors—such as inadequate sleep and home environmental hazards—can help inform the design of targeted fall-prevention strategies. Integrating sleep assessment into geriatric health services, improving home safety, and promoting physical activity could reduce the risk of falls and support healthy aging. The results may therefore help guide health professionals and community-based programs in developing evidence-based interventions to enhance the safety and well-being of older adults.
sections.conclusion: This study is among the nationally representative studies in Turkey to examine the relationship between sleep duration and falls among older adults, while comprehensively considering sociodemographic, lifestyle, clinical, and environmental factors. The findings of this study demonstrated that short nighttime sleep duration (< 7 h) was significantly associated with an increased risk of falls among older adults in Turkey. This association remained robust even after adjusting for a wide range of sociodemographic, lifestyle, clinical, psychosocial, and environmental factors. In contrast, long sleep duration (> 8 h) was not independently associated with fall risk after full adjustment, suggesting that previously observed associations may be confounded by underlying health conditions or functional impairments. Also, these findings highlight the importance of recognizing short sleep duration as a potentially modifiable risk factor for falls in aging populations. Public health strategies that promote healthy and adequate sleep may contribute to fall prevention and enhance the well-being of older adults. Of note, because falls have multifactorial causes, effective prevention requires a multidisciplinary approach engaging diverse healthcare providers, reinforcing that collaborative multi-domain interventions are essential to protect older adults from falls. Furthermore, recognizing and addressing depressive symptoms in individuals with poor sleep may help reduce both psychological burden and physical vulnerability. Integrating mental health perspectives into routine care is essential for identifying at-risk populations early and improving overall geriatric health outcomes. Further longitudinal studies are needed to clarify the causal mechanisms linking sleep duration and fall risk.
